name: Amy Levy
bio: Anglo-Jewish poet and novelist, born Amy Judith Levy in London on 10 November 1861, the second of seven children of a stockbroker; in 1879 she became the second Jewish woman to attend Cambridge and the first at Newnham College. Wilde published her while he edited the Woman's World: her story appeared in the first number, followed by articles on Christina Rossetti's poetry (March 1888) and on women and club life (June 1888), and two poems and a story during 1889. His one surviving letter to her, of October 1887, solicits more of her fiction - "I think your method as admirable as it is unique" - and after her death he printed a tribute to her in the same magazine, judging that she had "ceased to hold the orthodox doctrines of her nation, retaining, however, a strong race feeling"; she is one of the very few women on this map whose tie to Wilde is professional, mutual, and documented in his own hand. At Florence in 1886 she met Vernon Lee and fell in love with her, sending her the sonnet "To Vernon Lee" and the poem "New Love, New Life"; her biographer Linda Hunt Beckman calls these love poems. She took her own life on 10 September 1889, aged twenty-seven.
bio_note: Note a discrepancy in the Wilde apparatus: the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter to her, Complete Letters (2000), p. 326, gives her dates as "(1862-89)" - a year late on the birth. The Woman's World bibliography and the manner of death ("She committed suicide by inhaling fumes of charcoal") are from that same footnote. The Wilde tribute and the quoted sentence from it are Beckman's, who dates the tribute to an 1890 issue of the Woman's World; the quotation is Beckman quoting Wilde.
